ImageDescription.value:
Tawa or ype Mask. Tawa ceremony is one of the most complex rituals. This is a staging of ancient battles with neighboring tribes. During the ceremony, the spirit of the enemy incarnate by the mask ype. This type of mask is made by men in secret in the men's house. The Tawa is celebrated at the beginning of the dry season in several distinct phases. The first step is to appoint two emcees that must descend from a parent who killed an enemy. The second phase is the production of wooden masks. Sculpture trays is to give them an anthropomorphic figure. The plate is covered with feathers macaw whose combination of colors blazoned the identity of the group of which the mind of the enemy killed. The masks are kept in the men's house to celebrate the third phase of the ritual that features the old tribal wars and ended with the victory of Api'awa on their enemies.
Population : Apyawa / Tapirape - Brazil, Mato Grosso, Indigenous Land of Urubu Branco
Materials : Macaw feathers, ipe wood (tabebuia sp.), nacre, wax, cotton yarn
Size :43 x 81 x 7 cm

ImageDescription.value:
Post Tower, Bonn, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
The Post Tower is the tallest building in Bonn and a landmark of the modern federal district. After the parliament and government moved to Berlin, Bonn developed into the headquarters of international organizations and large companies.
At the end of the 1990s, Deutsche Post DHL Group decided to establish its corporate headquarters here. Construction began in 2000 based on plans by architect Helmut Jahn. The glass tower, which is approximately 162 meters high, was completed in 2002. Its striking double facade and transparent architecture are intended to symbolize openness and internationality.
The Post Tower represents Bonn’s economic transformation from the former federal capital to an important service and UN location.

ImageDescription.value:
Tram (railcar 65) in the Stadthaus 3, Münster, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
The tram system in Münster operated from July 13, 1901, to November 25, 1954. It was run by Stadtwerke Münster. At its peak, it comprised three lines and initially covered 8 kilometers, increasing to 12 kilometers in 1913. The routes ran from the Alter Schützenhof to Warendorfer Straße (yellow line, line 2 from 1925), from Marienplatz to the tram depot on Albersloher Weg (green line, line 3 from 1925) and from Steinfurter Straße through the northern part of the city to the main railway station (red line, line 1 from 1925). For a short time, there was also a fourth line from Marienplatz to Albersloher Weg (green line), which was later taken over by the red line.
Only the former Gotha tram motor car 65 has survived in its original form. In 1993, it found its way back to Münster in poor condition and was extensively restored from 2002 onwards by the Association for the Preservation of the Last Tram in Münster, which was founded in the same year. After successful restoration, the car found a home in the courtyard of Stadthaus 3 on September 30, 2013.

ImageDescription.value:
Wildlife park in Dülmen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
The wildlife park was designed in 1864 by English landscape architect Edward Milner as the “Amended Plan of Park Dülmen Westphalia” and laid out in 1868 by Charles Barnard, a gardener who also came from England. It is a classic landscape park with extensive meadows and a system of circular paths, which is also used for forestry. The park features the Herzteich pond with a small island, the moat of the former Schultenhof Hinderkinck farm, and a forester’s lodge near the moat. At the end of the 19th century, among other things, the park was expanded through the acquisition of additional properties. With the construction of the Bundesautobahn 43 in the 1970s, it was reduced in size by approximately 250 hectares.

ImageDescription.value: Female Wandering crab spider (Philodromus aureolus) with her egg sac, Hartelholz forest, Munich, Germany. This specimen is a 6 millimetres (0.24 in) long tiny spider and is widespread in western and central Europe.
